q: Do modern QAOA variants (warm-start QAOA, ADAPT-QAOA, XY-mixer QAOA, recursive QAOA) actually beat vanilla QAOA on the exact instance families Willsch et al. benchmarked, or do the gains reported in the variant literature disappear when tested on this specific 3-regular / ER / weighted-MaxCut / 2-SAT suite?
basis: Willsch et al. only benchmark the original 2014 QAOA (Farhi--Goldstone--Gutmann) formulation. The QAOA literature since 2020 has produced several variants that claim depth-p advantages at the same p, but they are typically evaluated on custom instance sets that are not the Willsch suite. A same-suite head-to-head is missing.
next_steps: (1) Extend code/qaoa_maxcut.py to instantiate warm-start QAOA (GW rounding as initial state), ADAPT-QAOA (grow mixer pool adaptively), and the XY-mixer variant on the same 6 graphs at p=1..5. (2) Report deltas in alpha and P_ground vs the vanilla numbers already in evidence/qaoa_results.json. (3) Free simulator only; runtime should still be minutes on a laptop for n<=10.

q: How does realistic hardware noise (depolarising + T1/T2 + measurement) perturb the monotone-p-improvement trend reported here? Is there a p* beyond which noise wins and the alpha vs p curve turns over on current-generation superconducting hardware?
basis: The paper's C6 (IBM Q p=1 landscape is noisier than the simulator) is a hardware qualitative observation. It does not answer at what p noise overwhelms the algorithmic gain. Our noiseless statevector shows monotone improvement, but this trivially cannot show the turnover.
next_steps: Rerun the same instance suite through qiskit-aer's noise-model pipeline with FakeSherbrooke / FakeQuebec (127-qubit IBM device noise models, free) at p=1..6. Plot alpha(p) with and without noise on the same axes. This is a free-simulator experiment; only additional cost is ~10x wall-clock over the noiseless run.

q: On the exact 3-regular and Erdos-Renyi instances used here, how does QAOA at its best-observed depth (p=3, alpha in [0.87, 0.95]) compare to a modern classical baseline (Goemans-Williamson SDP rounding, simulated annealing with a fair budget, tabu search)? Is there any instance in the suite where QAOA-p3 beats every classical baseline at matched compute budget?
basis: The replication reports alpha~0.95 at p=3 but does not run any classical baseline on the same graphs. Without a classical anchor the numbers are not actionable as quantum-advantage evidence. Willsch et al. anchor with D-Wave, not with SDP/SA.
next_steps: Add code/classical_baselines.py running (a) cvxpy-based Goemans-Williamson (many free implementations exist) with 100 random-hyperplane rounds; (b) SA via networkx or a 30-line Metropolis loop with a budget matched to QAOA's optimizer function-eval count; (c) tabu search (mqlib is free). Emit a per-graph comparison table alongside the existing per-instance table.

q: Does the paper's headline trend transfer to weighted MaxCut and to constrained MaxCut (MaxCut with cardinality or partition-size constraints)? The paper's Fig. of weighted-MaxCut curves is not replicated here.
basis: This replication only exercised unweighted MaxCut. Weighted MaxCut was one of the paper's two headline problem families. Constrained variants (e.g. balanced cut) are common in practice but require penalty-Hamiltonian encodings that change the QAOA landscape.
next_steps: Add a weighted 3-regular generator (edge weights ~ Uniform(0,1) or Gaussian) matching the paper's Sec.~III weighting scheme, rerun the p=1..3 sweep, and separately encode a k-balanced MaxCut penalty into H_C for the same graphs. Compare monotone-p behaviour to the unweighted numbers.

q: Can ML-boosted / transfer-learning parameter initialisation (e.g. Zhou et al.'s parameter concentration on 3-regular MaxCut, graph-neural-network warm starts, or optimal-parameter reuse across graph sizes) reduce the number of COBYLA function evaluations to reach the alpha values reported here, and do those savings hold beyond the small-n regime this replication tested?
basis: Parameter concentration on 3-regular MaxCut (near-identical optimal (gamma, beta) across instance sizes) is a well-known phenomenon post-2018; if it holds on our suite, we could initialise COBYLA at a fixed (gamma_0, beta_0) and skip the random-restart step entirely, materially reducing the wall-clock. Whether the concentration extends to Erdos-Renyi and to weighted MaxCut is less established.
next_steps: (1) Extract optimal (gamma*, beta*) for each 3-regular instance at p=1,2,3 from evidence/qaoa_results.json and check parameter concentration (variance across seeds). (2) Try transferring the mean parameter from n=6 to warm-start n=8, n=10 optimizers; measure alpha achieved and function-eval count. (3) Free experiment; pure post-processing of existing evidence plus a small extra run.
